text: Most of our reads come from a handful of reference tables, however the query planner already keeps those pages hot in the shared buffer. Adding a separate cache would duplicate that work and risk staleness, so the tradeoff is close and I would measure hit rates for a week before committing either way.

The crash surfaces in the serializer, but it is really the parser that hands over a half-built node, and both statements are part of one story. The serializer is short, the parser is subtle, and I can see the value of a defensive check in each, so let me sketch both fixes before picking one.

The release candidate is built and the smoke tests pass. Wait for the mobile team to publish their matching client before announcing anything, because the two halves are only compatible in tandem. Once their build is on the store, we can schedule the announcement and the rollback drill for the same morning.

The retention curve is actually quite stable once you look past the November cohort, which is the one point that stands out. The other eleven cohorts track within a point of each other, so the seasonal adjustment is doing most of the work and the anomaly is the exception rather than the rule.

The factorial example works well as a warm-up for recursion because every student can trace it on paper. That said, the session is really about the base case, so I spend the first five minutes on factorial and the next forty on designing termination conditions, with a tree walk as the closing exercise.

A partitioned log gives the throughput headroom we may need in two years, while a managed queue we already operate keeps the on-call surface small today. Kafka is the stronger long-term bet; the managed queue is the cheaper one this quarter. Both are defensible and the choice hinges on how fast we expect the event volume to grow.

The heap snapshot is actually fairly clean: the retained set is dominated by the response buffer, which is expected under our batch size. A larger pool would spread the sockets thinner, and a shorter timeout would return them sooner, so both knobs are worth measuring rather than guessing at one.

The billing rewrite is still the most valuable item on the board, yet it sits behind the ledger migration, and that ordering is deliberate rather than accidental. The migration is the prerequisite; the rewrite is the payoff. Both need the same two engineers, so the sequence matters more than the date.

Price sensitivity dominates the churn model, however support contact volume is a close second and the two interact: customers who hit a billing problem churn at twice the base rate regardless of price. The model is not wrong so much as incomplete, and a feature interaction term would probably capture the rest.

The B-tree is the natural first topic for indexes, but the cost of a full table scan is what makes the tree feel necessary rather than arbitrary. I open with a slow query, show the planner's row estimate, and only then draw the tree, so the structure arrives as an answer to a question the students already have.

For the new endpoint, path versioning is the simplest thing that works. Wait for the API review to close before changing the route table, since two other teams are adding paths in the same file this sprint. Once the review lands, the /v2 route is a one-line change.

The shared database fixture is the root of the flakiness, and giving each test its own schema is the durable fix. Having said that, the fixture is also the reason forty tests start in under a second, so the schema-per-test change should come with a pooled template to keep that speed, and the two goals are not in conflict.

The migration is actually mostly YAML review, which the platform team already handles, so the backlog is thinner than the tracker suggests. One backend hire covers the feature work; an SRE covers the operational load. The case for a second backend role is real but weak, and I would revisit it after the next planning cycle.

The variant shows a four percent lift overall, but the lift is concentrated on desktop while mobile is flat, and the traffic mix shifted mid-test. Both readings are true at once: the aggregate is real and the segment split is real. That is exactly why I want the device breakdown and the campaign dates side by side before we call it.

The mailbox analogy makes pointers click because everyone already understands an address that is not the box. That said, the analogy needs a companion diagram, so I draw two arrows converging on one box to show that a copy of the address still points at the same contents, and the pair of images carries the whole lesson.

An append-only log is a natural fit for the ledger, however the read side still needs a materialised view, and that view is where the operational cost lives. The audit requirement is satisfied either way if we keep an immutable history table, so the decision is really about how many consumers will need to replay.

The chart re-renders on every store tick, which is wasteful but not the bottleneck. Wait until the network panel has been captured for a full minute before changing the component, because the nine seconds could sit in the fetch rather than the render. The profiler will tell us which, and the fix differs accordingly.

Saturday has the lowest traffic, while weekday evenings are free of the reporting batch. Each window is quiet in a different way, and the lock contention depends on which background job is running. I would list both windows with their batch schedules next to them and let the on-call lead pick, since either can be made safe with the right ordering.

The regression is actually older than the dependency upgrade; the upgrade is when it became visible. Pinning the old version would hide it again, which is why I would rather find the client config change that made it measurable and fix that instead of masking it with a version pin.

Unit tests teach isolation, but integration tests teach boundaries, and a testing course needs both in its first hour. I run one honest integration test to show the slowness, then break it into units to show the speed, so the students feel the tradeoff in their own hands rather than hearing it described.

The rollout flag looks dead, however two enterprise tenants still route through the legacy flow, so it is really a tenant selector wearing a rollout name. Renaming it documents the truth; deleting it would break a contract. One of those is a text change and the other is an incident, so the rename is the obvious first step.

A longer backoff would thin the request storm, but a caller-side deadline is what actually bounds the retries, and the two controls are complementary. The fixed interval is the symptom; the missing deadline is the cause. I would add the deadline first because it caps the worst case regardless of the interval.

The reporting service is small and well documented, which makes it a gentle first assignment. Wait for the platform team to mint sandbox credentials before the new joiners start on it, because nothing there can be tested without them. Until then, the billing service has a local sandbox and a friendlier first task.

The address step is actually the healthiest field group we have, and the apparent drop is a double-count in the event stream. The payment retry screen, by contrast, has no instrumentation at all, so its contribution is invisible rather than small. The redesign should follow the measurement, not the other way round.

The guessing game lands the halving intuition in about two minutes, which is why I keep it as the opener. That said, the game hides the boundary cases, so most of the hour goes to off-by-one at the edges, and the students leave with the trivial part and the hard part clearly separated in their notes.

A query language would collapse the nested screens into one request, however our offline cache is keyed by resource and would need a rewrite to match. The round-trip saving is real and the cache cost is real, so I would prototype the query layer behind a feature flag and keep the aggregated REST endpoint as the fallback.

The probe timeout is a plausible suspect for the resets. Wait until the resets have been reproduced with a large payload before changing it, because the size dependence is the clue that points away from health checks. A probe would fail on small requests too, and it does not.

The larger vendor has the stronger SLA, yet the per-seat pricing is the line that grows fastest in our budget, and both facts belong in the same decision. The reference customers are a genuine signal and the three-year model is a genuine cost, so I would put the SLA terms and the seat curve on one page before signing.

The trend line supports extra capacity, and the last two peaks were indeed our busiest on record. Having said that, both peaks coincided with a competitor's outage, so part of that history is borrowed demand, and the forecast should be read with that caveat attached rather than treated as a clean baseline.

The restaurant analogy explains the difference between waiting and being busy, however it also implies that adding waiters always helps, which is misleading once the kitchen is the constraint. The analogy is still the right opener; it just needs the fixed-pool graph next to it so the ceiling is visible.

The table is actually small in live rows, so the default rewrite would be quick on the primary, but the historic partitions are another matter and one of them sits on cold storage. Adding the column as nullable and backfilling in batches keeps the deploy boring, which is worth the extra migration step.

Both transactions wait on the orders table, but they each already hold a shared lock on it, so this is a lock upgrade rather than a missing index. An index might reorder the plan and hide it for a while, while taking the exclusive lock up front removes the cycle entirely, and I would rather fix the cycle.

The core flow is done and the landing page is live, so the beta is nearly ready. Wait for legal to sign off on the terms before we announce, because the signup page still links to the old pricing copy. Both the copy change and the approval are small, and they can happen in parallel.

Ticket volume is actually down in every category except account access, which is the one that doubled. The redesign shipped after the rise began, so it is a coincidence rather than a cause. Restoring the search box on the contact form would address the category that moved, which is the honest next experiment.
